questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design and implement monitoring and alerting solutions for an AWS account or organization
questions.question: A company runs dozens of AWS accounts in AWS Organizations and wants Amazon GuardDuty threat detection managed by the security team. Findings from every member account must be managed from one security tooling account rather than the management account. Accounts that join the organization later must be covered by GuardDuty without anyone enabling it account by account. What should the security team configure?
options: Designate the security tooling account as GuardDuty administrator and send invitations to each member account as it joins.
Enable GuardDuty separately in each member account and forward the findings to the security tooling account with Amazon EventBridge.
Enable GuardDuty in the management account and use it to manage findings for each member account as accounts join.
Designate the security tooling account as the delegated GuardDuty administrator and set auto-enable to cover all member accounts.
questions.correct_rationale: A delegated administrator in the tooling account manages findings, and auto-enable for all members covers accounts that join later.
distractor_rationales: The tooling account manages findings, but invitations sent account by account do not cover joining accounts automatically.
Per-account enablement with forwarding needs manual work for every new account and sets up no organization administrator.
Auto coverage could be arranged, but findings are managed from the management account instead of the security tooling account.
questions.distractor_summary: WA uses the management account; WB invites accounts one by one; X enables per account and forwards.

docLinks.title: Managing GuardDuty accounts with AWS Organizations

questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design and implement monitoring and alerting solutions for an AWS account or organization
questions.question: A security operations team uses AWS Security Hub CSPM in four AWS Regions and reviews findings by switching consoles. Analysts must review and update findings from all four Regions in a single Security Hub CSPM view. The team does not want to build or maintain custom code that copies findings between Regions. Which approach meets these requirements?
options: Keep Security Hub CSPM separate in each Region and give analysts saved console bookmarks for every Region.
Export Security Hub CSPM findings from each Region to Amazon S3 and query them together with Amazon Athena.
Write a Lambda function in each Region that copies Security Hub CSPM findings into a table in one Region.
Turn on Security Hub CSPM cross-Region aggregation with one home Region and link the other Regions to it.
questions.correct_rationale: Cross-Region aggregation replicates findings from linked Regions into the home Region view without custom code.
distractor_rationales: Bookmarks avoid custom code, but analysts still switch Regions and lack one Security Hub CSPM view.
Exported findings in Athena need a custom pipeline and are not updated inside a Security Hub CSPM view.
A copying Lambda function centralizes findings, but it is custom code the team must build and maintain.
questions.distractor_summary: WA builds custom copy code; WB keeps Regions separate; X exports outside Security Hub CSPM.

questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design and implement monitoring and alerting solutions for an AWS account or organization
questions.question: A company stores several petabytes across hundreds of Amazon S3 buckets and needs to know which buckets likely hold personal data. The assessment must keep running as new buckets and objects appear, with no one defining a job per bucket. Cost must stay controlled, so every object in every bucket must not be fully scanned. Which Amazon Macie approach meets these requirements?
options: Create one recurring Macie job that scans every object in every bucket each day to find personal data.
Enable Macie automated sensitive data discovery so it evaluates the bucket inventory and samples representative objects.
Turn on Amazon GuardDuty S3 Protection so it reports which objects in each bucket hold personal data.
Create a Macie sensitive data discovery job for each bucket and schedule each job to rerun whenever new objects arrive in it.
questions.correct_rationale: Automated discovery keeps evaluating new buckets and samples objects, which avoids full scans of every object.
distractor_rationales: One recurring job needs no per-bucket setup, but scanning every object daily breaks the cost requirement.
GuardDuty S3 Protection detects threats to buckets and does not classify objects as personal data.
Per-bucket jobs can limit scope, but someone must define a job for every bucket as new ones appear.
questions.distractor_summary: WA needs per-bucket jobs; WB scans everything; X uses a threat detection service.

docLinks.title: Performing automated sensitive data discovery

questions.subdomain: 1.2 Design and implement logging solutions
questions.question: A company uses AWS Organizations and must keep an audit record of API activity for every account. API events for the management account and every member account must be captured by one trail configuration. Member account administrators must not be able to stop or delete the logging for their own account. How should the security engineer set up the logging?
options: Enable AWS Config in each account and use the configuration history as the audit record of API activity.
Create an organization trail and also grant member account administrators permission to stop logging when needed.
Create an organization trail from the management account so it logs events for the management and member accounts.
Create a trail in each member account with AWS CloudFormation StackSets and let local account administrators manage it.
questions.correct_rationale: An organization trail covers all accounts from one configuration and is not controlled by member account administrators.
distractor_rationales: AWS Config records resource configuration changes and is not a record of every API call.
The organization trail captures every account, but granting administrators stop permission breaks the second requirement.
StackSets spread trails, but each account has its own trail that local administrators can stop or delete.
questions.distractor_summary: WA uses per-account trails; WB lets members stop logging; X uses configuration history.

docLinks.title: Creating a trail for an organization

questions.subdomain: 1.2 Design and implement logging solutions
questions.question: A security team collects AWS CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and Route 53 resolver logs and wants to analyze them together with partner tools. The logs from different sources must be stored in one standard open-source schema so analysts can join them. The team does not want to write and run its own transformation jobs to normalize each log source. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Send all logs to one Amazon S3 bucket in their native formats and let analysts join them with Athena.
Use Amazon Security Lake so the ingested logs are converted to Apache Parquet in the OCSF schema.
Write AWS Glue jobs that read each log source and transform the records into the OCSF schema.
Stream all logs into CloudWatch Logs and use Logs Insights queries to analyze the sources side by side.
questions.correct_rationale: Security Lake normalizes ingested sources into OCSF in Parquet, so no custom transformation jobs are needed.
distractor_rationales: One bucket avoids transformation work, but native formats leave the sources in different schemas.
Glue jobs can produce OCSF records, but they are transformation jobs the team must write and run.
CloudWatch Logs keeps each source in its own format and does not apply a standard schema.
questions.distractor_summary: WA keeps native formats; WB writes transformation jobs; X keeps separate formats in CloudWatch Logs.

docLinks.title: What is Amazon Security Lake?

questions.subdomain: 1.2 Design and implement logging solutions
questions.question: A security engineer must record the DNS queries that workloads in selected VPCs make, along with the responses. Which feature provides this record?
options: AWS CloudTrail data events configured for Route 53 so that each DNS lookup from the VPCs is recorded.
VPC Flow Logs configured on the subnets so that every DNS lookup and its answer is captured in the log.
Amazon Route 53 Resolver query logging configured for the VPCs whose DNS queries and responses must be recorded.
Route 53 public hosted zone query logging configured so that the lookups made by the selected VPC workloads are recorded.
questions.correct_rationale: Resolver query logging records queries that originate in the VPCs you specify and the responses to them.
distractor_rationales: CloudTrail records API calls, not the DNS lookups that workloads make.
Flow logs capture IP traffic metadata, not the DNS query names and responses.
Public hosted zone logging records queries that reach a public zone, not all lookups from chosen VPCs.
questions.distractor_summary: Flow logs capture packets metadata; CloudTrail records API calls; public zone logging covers only public zones.

questions.subdomain: 1.3 Troubleshoot security monitoring, logging, and alerting solutions
questions.question: An engineer creates a VPC flow log that publishes to a CloudWatch Logs log group, but the flow log shows an access error and no records arrive. The IAM role for the flow log already has a permissions policy that allows writing to CloudWatch Logs. The fix must keep the flow log publishing to CloudWatch Logs rather than switching the destination. What is the most likely fix?
options: Add a resource policy to the CloudWatch Logs log group that grants the VPC itself write access.
Add more CloudWatch Logs write actions to the IAM role permissions policy used by the flow log.
Update the IAM role trust policy so the flow logs service is allowed to assume the role.
Change the flow log destination to an Amazon S3 bucket so that no IAM role is needed for delivery.
questions.correct_rationale: With write permissions present, a missing trust relationship for the flow logs service stops delivery.
distractor_rationales: A VPC is not a principal, and the flow logs service still needs to assume the role.
The permissions policy already allows writing, so more write actions do not fix a role the service cannot assume.
An S3 destination could work, but it breaks the requirement to keep publishing to CloudWatch Logs.
questions.distractor_summary: WA repeats existing permissions; WB changes destination; X grants a non-principal.

docLinks.title: IAM role for publishing flow logs to CloudWatch Logs

questions.subdomain: 1.3 Troubleshoot security monitoring, logging, and alerting solutions
questions.question: A team enabled CloudWatch execution logging for a REST API in one Region and it works, then deployed the same API to a second Region. In the second Region, enabling execution logging on the stage fails with an error about a missing CloudWatch role. The fix must keep execution logs in CloudWatch Logs in the second Region for the deployed stage. What should the team do?
options: Set the cloudWatchRoleArn property in the API Gateway account settings of the second Region to the logging role.
Recreate the logging IAM role in the second Region because IAM roles are scoped to the Region where they are made.
Attach the CloudWatch logging policy to the IAM user who deploys the REST API stage in the second Region.
Turn off execution logging in the second Region and rely on access logging sent to Amazon Data Firehose.
questions.correct_rationale: The CloudWatch role ARN is an account setting per Region, so the second Region needs its own cloudWatchRoleArn.
distractor_rationales: IAM roles are global, so the existing role can be reused once the second Region references it.
The deploying user's permissions are not what API Gateway uses to write execution logs to CloudWatch Logs.
Firehose access logs avoid the error, but execution logs stop going to CloudWatch Logs in that Region.
questions.distractor_summary: WA drops execution logs; WB grants the wrong principal; X misreads IAM scope.

docLinks.title: Set up CloudWatch logging for REST APIs in API Gateway

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design and test an incident response plan
questions.question: A security team wants to test whether its incident response runbooks work when instances in a production workload fail. The test must inject real disruptions into the production workload through a managed AWS service. The test must stop on its own if a business health alarm goes into alarm during the experiment. Which approach meets these requirements?
options: Run an AWS FIS experiment against the production workload with a stop condition tied to the health alarm.
Run a tabletop exercise where responders walk through the runbooks against the production workload on paper.
Run an AWS FIS experiment against a copy of the workload in a test account with no stop condition.
Write a script on an EC2 instance that stops production instances and let an engineer end it by hand.
questions.correct_rationale: FIS injects managed disruptions into production and its stop conditions end the experiment on the alarm.
distractor_rationales: A tabletop exercise has value, but it injects no real disruption into the production workload.
FIS is managed, but a test copy is not production, and no stop condition ties to the health alarm.
A custom script disrupts production, but it is not a managed service and has no automatic stop.
questions.distractor_summary: WA injects nothing; WB is unmanaged with no auto stop; X tests a copy without a stop condition.

docLinks.title: What is AWS Fault Injection Service?

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design and test an incident response plan
questions.question: A security team writes a containment runbook that isolates a compromised instance and must also call internal ticketing logic written in Python. The custom Python logic must run as a step inside the same Systems Manager Automation runbook. The team does not want to manage a separate compute service just to host the Python step. How should the team build the runbook step?
options: Add a Run Command step that sends the Python script to the compromised instance and runs it there.
Deploy the Python logic as a separate Lambda function and have the runbook call that function as a step.
Keep the Python logic on an EC2 helper instance and have an engineer run it after the runbook finishes.
Add an aws:executeScript step to the Automation runbook that runs the custom Python function directly.
questions.correct_rationale: The aws:executeScript action runs the Python function inside the runbook without another compute service to manage.
distractor_rationales: Run Command executes on the compromised instance, which is not a separate step host and is risky to trust.
A Lambda step runs Python, but it is a separate compute service the team must deploy and manage.
A helper instance is another compute resource to manage and runs outside the runbook.
questions.distractor_summary: WA adds a separate compute service; WB runs on the compromised host; X runs outside the runbook.

docLinks.title: AWS Systems Manager Automation

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design and test an incident response plan
questions.question: A security team receives many Security Hub CSPM findings from a sandbox account that its response plan treats as low priority. Findings from the sandbox account must have their severity lowered automatically as they arrive in Security Hub CSPM. The team wants to do this inside Security Hub CSPM without building EventBridge rules and Lambda code. What should the team configure?
options: Create an EventBridge rule for sandbox findings that invokes a Lambda function to update each finding severity value.
Ask analysts to filter the sandbox account out of the Security Hub CSPM console each time they triage.
Disable the Security Hub CSPM standards in the sandbox account so that no findings arrive from it.
Create a Security Hub CSPM automation rule that matches the sandbox account ID and updates the finding severity.
questions.correct_rationale: Automation rules match criteria such as account ID and apply actions like a severity update inside Security Hub CSPM.
distractor_rationales: EventBridge and Lambda can update severity, but that is the custom build the team wants to avoid.
Console filters hide findings for one analyst and change no severity automatically.
Disabling standards removes the findings instead of lowering their severity as they arrive.
questions.distractor_summary: WA builds custom code; WB removes findings; X relies on manual filters.

docLinks.title: Understanding automation rules in Security Hub CSPM

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Respond to security events
questions.question: A responder removes all inbound rules from the security group of a compromised EC2 instance, but an attacker shell session stays open. The existing attacker session must be cut off while the instance is kept running for memory forensics. The containment must be done with network controls rather than by changing software on the instance. What should the responder do?
options: Stop the EC2 instance so the attacker session ends before the security group change is made again.
Add a network ACL deny for the traffic on the instance subnet, since tracked security group connections persist.
Log in to the instance and kill the attacker process so the session ends while the instance keeps running.
Remove the outbound rules from the same security group as well so that the tracked attacker session is dropped at once.
questions.correct_rationale: Security group changes leave tracked connections open, while a network ACL deny stops the traffic with the instance running.
distractor_rationales: Stopping the instance ends the session, but memory needed for forensics is lost.
Killing the process changes software on the instance rather than using network controls.
Further security group edits still leave the tracked connection in place, so the session continues.
questions.distractor_summary: WA loses memory; WB still relies on tracking; X changes software on the host.

docLinks.title: Amazon EC2 security group connection tracking

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Respond to security events
questions.question: After a GuardDuty finding, an analyst wants a service that helps investigate the activity and identify its root cause. Which service fits?
options: Amazon Inspector, which helps analyze and investigate security findings and identify the source of suspicious network activity.
Amazon Macie, which helps analyze stored data and investigate findings to identify the cause of suspicious activity.
Amazon Detective, which helps analyze and investigate security findings and identify the root cause of suspicious activity.
AWS Trusted Advisor, which helps analyze account checks and identify the cause of suspicious activity in findings.
questions.correct_rationale: Detective is built to analyze, investigate, and find the root cause of security findings.
distractor_rationales: Inspector scans workloads for vulnerabilities and does not investigate findings to a root cause.
Macie discovers sensitive data in S3 and does not investigate the root cause of findings.
Trusted Advisor gives best-practice checks and is not an investigation service.
questions.distractor_summary: Inspector scans vulnerabilities; Trusted Advisor gives checks; Macie classifies data.

docLinks.title: What is Amazon Detective?

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Respond to security events
questions.question: Temporary credentials from an IAM role used by an application were leaked, and the attacker is calling AWS APIs with them. All credentials issued for the role before now must stop working immediately. The application must keep working with new sessions of the same role after the response. What should the responder do?
options: Shorten the maximum session duration on the role so the leaked credentials expire sooner than planned.
Rotate the access keys of the IAM users who can assume the role so new sessions use the new keys.
Use the revoke active sessions feature on the role so credentials issued before now are denied all actions.
Delete the IAM role so that all of its issued credentials stop working, then recreate a new role for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: Revoking sessions denies credentials issued before the chosen time while new sessions of the same role keep working.
distractor_rationales: A shorter maximum duration affects new sessions and does not cut off credentials already issued.
Rotating user keys does not invalidate the role session credentials that already leaked.
Deleting the role stops old credentials but breaks the application, which depends on the same role.
questions.distractor_summary: WA breaks the role; WB does not affect issued credentials; X rotates the wrong credentials.

docLinks.title: Revoke IAM role temporary security credentials

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Respond to security events
questions.question: During an investigation, analysts must search months of CloudTrail log files stored in an Amazon S3 bucket for actions by one role. The analysts must run SQL queries against the log files where they already sit in Amazon S3. No servers or clusters may be provisioned for the investigation queries. Which approach meets these requirements?
options: Download the CloudTrail log files from S3 to a laptop and search them with a command line text tool.
Use the CloudTrail event history in the console to search the months of events for the role by name.
Create an Athena table whose LOCATION points to the CloudTrail logs in S3 and query it with SQL.
Load the CloudTrail log files from S3 into an Amazon Redshift provisioned cluster and query them with SQL.
questions.correct_rationale: Athena queries the logs in place in S3 with SQL and needs no servers or clusters.
distractor_rationales: A laptop search is not SQL against the logs in S3 and does not scale to months of logs.
Event history is a console search that is not SQL over the S3 log files.
Redshift runs SQL, but it moves the logs out of S3 and needs a provisioned cluster.
questions.distractor_summary: WA needs a cluster; WB leaves SQL and S3; X is a console search.

docLinks.title: Query AWS CloudTrail logs

questions.subdomain: 3.1 Design, implement, and troubleshoot security controls for network edge services
questions.question: A public login page behind an Application Load Balancer receives bursts of requests from a few client IP addresses trying many passwords. Requests from any single client IP address must be limited when that client sends too many requests too fast. Normal users from other IP addresses must keep reaching the login page during the bursts. Which control meets these requirements?
options: Add an AWS WAF rule on the load balancer that blocks all requests to the login page while a burst is happening.
Add an AWS WAF rate-based rule on the load balancer that rate limits each client IP sending requests too fast.
Lower the idle timeout on the Application Load Balancer so that clients sending bursts are disconnected sooner.
Add an IP set block rule in AWS WAF that lists the client IP addresses seen in the last burst of requests.
questions.correct_rationale: A rate-based rule counts requests per client IP and limits the fast ones while other users get through.
distractor_rationales: Blocking the whole login page during bursts also blocks normal users from other IP addresses.
An idle timeout change does not count requests or limit a client that sends them too fast.
A static IP set covers past attackers and does not limit new client IPs that start sending too fast.
questions.distractor_summary: WA blocks everyone; WB lists past IPs; X changes a timeout.

docLinks.title: Using rate-based rule statements in AWS WAF

questions.subdomain: 3.1 Design, implement, and troubleshoot security controls for network edge services
questions.question: A company serves static content from an Amazon S3 bucket through a CloudFront distribution and finds that users can also fetch objects straight from the bucket. Users must reach the objects through the CloudFront distribution and not directly from the S3 bucket. The S3 bucket must stay a private bucket with Block Public Access turned on. How should the engineer configure access?
options: Turn off Block Public Access and allow public reads in the bucket policy so CloudFront can fetch the objects.
Keep the bucket private and give users presigned S3 URLs so that they fetch the objects straight from S3.
Configure the S3 bucket as a static website endpoint origin and restrict it with a custom header from CloudFront.
Use origin access control on the distribution and allow that distribution in the private S3 bucket policy.
questions.correct_rationale: Origin access control signs CloudFront requests to the private bucket, so users cannot bypass the distribution.
distractor_rationales: Public reads let CloudFront fetch objects, but users can still read straight from the now public bucket.
Presigned URLs keep the bucket private, but users fetch from S3 instead of through CloudFront.
A website endpoint must be publicly readable, which breaks the private bucket requirement.
questions.distractor_summary: WA makes the bucket public; WB bypasses CloudFront; X needs a public website endpoint.

docLinks.title: Restrict access to an Amazon S3 origin

questions.subdomain: 3.1 Design, implement, and troubleshoot security controls for network edge services
questions.question: An application runs behind an internet-facing Application Load Balancer that is the origin for a CloudFront distribution with AWS WAF attached. Requests that skip CloudFront and go straight to the load balancer DNS name must not reach the application. Other CloudFront distributions owned by other AWS customers must not be able to reach the application either. Which configuration meets these requirements?
options: Make the Application Load Balancer internal so that requests to its DNS name from the internet cannot reach it.
Attach a second AWS WAF web ACL to the load balancer that allows requests with a CloudFront user agent string.
Allow the CloudFront managed prefix list in the load balancer security group and make no listener changes.
Have CloudFront add a secret custom header and set the listener to forward requests that carry that header.
questions.correct_rationale: A secret header added by this distribution and checked by the listener blocks direct calls and other distributions.
distractor_rationales: An internal load balancer cannot serve as this public CloudFront origin without other networking.
A user agent string is easy to forge and does not tie requests to this distribution.
The prefix list blocks direct internet calls, but any customer's CloudFront distribution can still reach the load balancer.
questions.distractor_summary: WA admits other distributions; WB breaks the origin; X trusts a forgeable header.

docLinks.title: Restrict access to Application Load Balancers

questions.subdomain: 3.2 Design, implement, and troubleshoot security controls for compute workloads
questions.question: Administrators connect to private EC2 instances through a bastion host with SSH keys, and auditors want that path removed. Administrators must still get interactive shell access to the private EC2 instances. No inbound ports may be opened and no SSH keys may be managed for this access. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Replace the bastion host with EC2 Instance Connect so administrators push temporary SSH keys over an open port.
Keep the bastion host but rotate the SSH keys monthly and restrict the inbound port to the corporate IP range.
Remove all shell access and require administrators to rebuild the private instances from images to make changes.
Use Systems Manager Session Manager to open shell sessions on the instances with no inbound ports or SSH keys.
questions.correct_rationale: Session Manager gives interactive shells without opening inbound ports or managing SSH keys.
distractor_rationales: Instance Connect pushes SSH keys over an inbound port, which breaks the no inbound port rule.
Restricting the bastion port still opens an inbound port and keeps SSH keys to manage.
Rebuilding from images removes the interactive shell access the administrators still need.
questions.distractor_summary: WA keeps ports and keys; WB keeps an open port; X removes shell access.

docLinks.title: AWS Systems Manager Session Manager

questions.subdomain: 3.2 Design, implement, and troubleshoot security controls for compute workloads
questions.question: A platform team pushes container images to a private Amazon ECR registry and wants known software vulnerabilities in packages reported. Images in the private registry must be scanned for package vulnerabilities by a managed AWS service. The findings must appear without the team installing scanning agents in the running containers. Which approach meets these requirements?
options: Set Amazon Inspector as the scanning service for the private registry so pushed images are checked for vulnerabilities.
Enable Amazon GuardDuty runtime monitoring so it reports package vulnerabilities in the images stored in the registry.
Run an open-source scanner inside each running container and send the package vulnerability results to a central S3 bucket.
Turn on AWS Config rules for the ECR repositories so that package vulnerabilities in the stored images are reported.
questions.correct_rationale: Inspector scans images in the private ECR registry for package vulnerabilities as a managed service with no agents.
distractor_rationales: GuardDuty runtime monitoring detects threats at runtime and does not report image package vulnerabilities.
A scanner in each running container needs agents in containers and is not a managed AWS service.
Config rules evaluate repository settings and do not scan image packages for vulnerabilities.
questions.distractor_summary: WA needs agents; WB is threat detection; X checks settings.

docLinks.title: Scanning Amazon Elastic Container Registry container images with Amazon Inspector

questions.subdomain: 3.2 Design, implement, and troubleshoot security controls for compute workloads
questions.question: A penetration test showed that a server-side request forgery flaw in a web app on EC2 could read role credentials from the instance metadata service. Simple GET requests to the metadata service, like those the flaw sends, must fail on the instance. The application must keep reading role credentials from the instance metadata service. What should the engineer configure on the instance?
options: Add a security group rule that blocks outbound traffic from the instance to the metadata service address.
Remove the IAM role from the instance and store long-term access keys in the application configuration file.
Set the instance metadata options to require IMDSv2 tokens so that IMDSv1 GET requests to the service fail.
Turn off the instance metadata service on the instance so that the flaw can no longer read any credentials.
questions.correct_rationale: Requiring IMDSv2 makes token-less GET calls fail while the app keeps getting credentials with session tokens.
distractor_rationales: Blocking the metadata address would also stop the app reading role credentials, which breaks the second requirement.
Long-term keys in a file are a worse credential risk and remove the metadata service use.
Turning off the metadata service stops the flaw but also stops the app reading role credentials.
questions.distractor_summary: WA breaks credential access; WB adds static keys; X uses a control that does not apply.

docLinks.title: Use the Instance Metadata Service to access instance metadata

questions.subdomain: 3.3 Design and troubleshoot network security controls
questions.question: A threat intelligence feed names a range of IP addresses that is attacking web servers in one public subnet. Traffic from that IP range must be explicitly denied for every instance in the subnet. The control must apply at the subnet level so new instances launched in the subnet are covered without changes. Which control meets these requirements?
options: Remove the route to the internet gateway from the subnet route table so that the attacking range cannot connect.
Associate a custom network ACL with the subnet that has an inbound deny rule for the attacking IP range.
Install a host firewall rule on each web server that drops packets from the attacking IP range at the instance.
Add a deny rule for the attacking IP address range to the security group used by each web server in the subnet.
questions.correct_rationale: Network ACLs support explicit deny rules and apply to every instance in the associated subnet.
distractor_rationales: Removing the internet route blocks every client, not just the attacking range.
Host firewall rules work per instance, so new instances need changes and the control is not subnet level.
Security groups support allow rules, so an explicit deny for the range cannot be written there.
questions.distractor_summary: WA cannot deny; WB blocks everyone; X is per instance.

docLinks.title: Control subnet traffic with network access control lists

questions.subdomain: 3.3 Design and troubleshoot network security controls
questions.question: Workloads in private subnets reach the internet through a NAT gateway, and security wants outbound HTTPS limited to a set of approved domain names. Outbound traffic must be allowed by domain name, because the approved services change their IP addresses often. The control must inspect traffic centrally for the VPC rather than relying on each workload. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Use network ACL outbound rules on the private subnets that allow the IP ranges resolved for each approved domain name.
Add the current IP addresses of the approved services to outbound security group rules on each workload instance.
Route outbound traffic through AWS Network Firewall with a stateful domain allow list for the approved names.
Configure a proxy setting in each workload that points to an allow list of the approved domain names it may call.
questions.correct_rationale: A stateful domain allow list in Network Firewall filters by name centrally, so IP changes do not matter.
distractor_rationales: Network ACLs match IP ranges, not names, so the allow list breaks when the addresses change.
Security group rules use IP addresses, which go stale as the services change their addresses.
Per-workload proxy settings filter by name, but they rely on each workload rather than a central control.
questions.distractor_summary: WA uses stale IPs; WB is per workload; X matches IP ranges.

docLinks.title: Stateful domain list rule groups in AWS Network Firewall

questions.subdomain: 3.3 Design and troubleshoot network security controls
questions.question: An auditor asks the security team to show which network paths exist from the internet to databases in a production VPC. The answer must come from analysis of the network configuration rather than from sending traffic to the databases. The team wants to define the access it considers unintended and have the service report matching paths. Which tool should the team use?
options: Run a port scan from an EC2 instance on the internet against the databases and record the ports that respond.
Enable VPC Flow Logs on the database subnets and look for accepted traffic that came from internet IP addresses.
Use Network Access Analyzer with a scope that defines internet to database paths and review the paths it finds.
Review the IAM policies attached to the database instances to find which principals can reach them over the network.
questions.correct_rationale: Network Access Analyzer evaluates configuration against a scope you define and reports unintended paths.
distractor_rationales: A port scan sends traffic to the databases instead of analyzing the network configuration.
Flow logs show traffic that happened, not every path the configuration allows.
IAM policies govern API permissions and do not describe network paths to the databases.
questions.distractor_summary: WA sends traffic; WB shows past traffic; X checks API permissions.

docLinks.title: What is Network Access Analyzer?

questions.subdomain: 4.1 Design, implement, and troubleshoot authentication strategies
questions.question: A company keeps its workforce identities in an external identity provider and wants employees to sign in to many AWS accounts. Employees must sign in with their existing identity provider credentials rather than separate AWS passwords. Users and groups must be provisioned into AWS automatically when they change in the identity provider. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Connect the external identity provider to IAM Identity Center with SAML for sign in and SCIM for provisioning.
Create an Amazon Cognito user pool federated to the identity provider and grant employees console access through it.
Create IAM users in every account for each employee and sync their passwords from the identity provider each night.
Connect the identity provider to IAM Identity Center with SAML and create the users and groups there by hand.

VPC Flow Logs on the worker node subnets, with Amazon Inspector scanning the container images that the clusters run.
GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring for the EKS clusters with automated agent management, so GuardDuty installs and updates the security agent.
GuardDuty EKS Protection for Kubernetes audit logs, which needs no agent and reports suspicious API activity against each cluster.

Flow logs and image scanning show traffic metadata and vulnerabilities, not runtime process and file behavior.
Audit log monitoring needs no agent, but it sees Kubernetes API calls rather than process and file activity inside containers.

questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design and implement monitoring and alerting solutions for an AWS account or organization
questions.question: A security operations team has CloudWatch alarms on metrics such as failed console sign-ins and root account usage. Each alarm that enters the ALARM state must create a work item that responders can track with its related resources until it is resolved. Responders must be able to run Systems Manager Automation runbooks against the affected resources from the same work item. Which solution meets these requirements?

Send the alarms to an Amazon SNS topic that emails the on-call responders, who then run Automation runbooks from the console.
Route the alarms through an EventBridge rule to a Lambda function that records each alarm as an item in a DynamoDB table.
Have the alarms create OpsItems in Systems Manager OpsCenter, and run Automation runbooks from each OpsItem.
questions.correct_rationale: OpsCenter creates a trackable OpsItem for each alarm, and responders can run Automation runbooks from the OpsItem.
distractor_rationales: Custom findings are visible, but they are not OpsItems and do not offer runbook execution against the resources.
Email alerts notify responders, but they create no tracked work item that holds the related resources until resolution.
A DynamoDB record can be tracked, but responders cannot run Automation runbooks from it and the team maintains the code.

questions.subdomain: 1.2 Design and implement logging solutions

The record must show each DeleteObject and DeleteObjects call made against objects in that bucket. The bucket serves millions of reads and uploads each day, and the team must keep CloudTrail costs under control. Which CloudTrail configuration meets these requirements?
options: Log all S3 data events for the bucket with basic event selectors, so that every read, upload, and deletion on the bucket is recorded.
Log management events of the Write type on the trail, which record the changes that are made to the bucket through the S3 API.
Turn on CloudTrail Insights for the trail so that unusual rates of deletion calls on the bucket are recorded.
Log S3 data events with advanced event selectors that match the bucket ARN and the DeleteObject and DeleteObjects event names.
questions.correct_rationale: Advanced selectors filtered on the bucket and the delete event names record each deletion without logging the heavy read and upload volume.
distractor_rationales: Logging every data event records the deletions, but it also logs millions of reads and uploads and raises costs.
Management events cover bucket-level operations, not object-level calls such as DeleteObject.
Insights flags unusual call rates, not a record of each individual object deletion.

questions.question: A security analyst wants to run SQL queries that join conditions on several fields of CloudTrail events kept in an immutable store. Which feature provides this?

CloudTrail Insights events, which record unusual API call rates and error rates that the trail detects in the account.
AWS CloudTrail Lake, which keeps events in event data stores and supports SQL queries across many event fields.
CloudTrail Event history in the console, filtered by one attribute such as the user name or the event name at a time.

distractor_rationales: Metric filters count matching log events; they do not run SQL across event fields.
Insights records unusual activity rates; it is not a SQL query store for events.
Event history filters on one attribute at a time and does not offer SQL queries.

questions.question: A central logging account receives application logs from workload accounts through CloudWatch Logs subscriptions to a destination in the N. The central team will keep a single Kinesis data stream in the N. Virginia Region for every Region. What should the central team do?

Create a CloudWatch Logs destination in the Ireland Region in the central account that targets the N. Virginia stream, and subscribe the Ireland log groups.
Schedule daily export tasks that copy the Ireland log groups to an S3 bucket in the central account for the team to load.
Subscribe the Ireland log groups directly to the existing N. Virginia destination in the central account, adding the workload accounts to its access policy.

distractor_rationales: This streams in near real time, but it adds a second stream instead of keeping a single stream in the N. Virginia Region.
Daily exports are batch copies and do not stream the logs in near real time.
A subscription cannot use a destination in another Region, because the log group and destination must share a Region.

questions.subdomain: 1.3 Troubleshoot security monitoring, logging, and alerting solutions
questions.question: EC2 instances in private subnets run the CloudWatch agent, but no logs arrive, and the agent log shows dial tcp i/o timeout errors to the CloudWatch Logs endpoint. The subnets must keep no route to the internet. Interface endpoints for CloudWatch and CloudWatch Logs exist with private DNS enabled, and their security group allows inbound traffic from the bastion host security group alone. What should the engineer change?
options: Turn on private DNS for the CloudWatch Logs interface endpoint so that the agent resolves the service name to the endpoint.
Add a NAT gateway and an internet route for the private subnets so that the agent can reach the public CloudWatch endpoints.
Add an inbound HTTPS rule to the endpoint security group that allows traffic from the agent instances' security group.
Attach a role with the CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy to the instances so the agent can sign its requests to CloudWatch Logs.
questions.correct_rationale: The timeouts mean the agent cannot reach the endpoint, and the endpoint security group admits the bastion but not the agent instances.
distractor_rationales: Private DNS is already enabled on the endpoints, so it does not explain the timeouts.
A NAT gateway would reach the public endpoints, but the subnets must keep no internet route.
A missing role causes access errors, not network timeouts to the endpoint.
questions.distractor_summary: WA adds an internet path; WB fixes DNS that already works; X fixes credentials, not reachability.

questions.subdomain: 1.3 Troubleshoot security monitoring, logging, and alerting solutions
questions.question: A team turned on CloudFront legacy standard logging to Amazon S3 and pointed it at the application's asset bucket, but no log files arrive. The team must keep using legacy standard logging with delivery to an S3 bucket in the same account. The asset bucket has S3 Object Ownership set to bucket owner enforced, and the security team requires ACLs to stay disabled on that bucket. What should the team do?
options: Create a separate log bucket with ACLs enabled in its Object Ownership setting, and deliver standard logs there.
Add a bucket policy to the asset bucket that allows the CloudFront service principal to put objects under a log prefix.
Change the asset bucket's Object Ownership setting to bucket owner preferred so that CloudFront can write log files there.
Switch the distribution to standard logging delivered to CloudWatch Logs so that logs arrive without an S3 bucket at all.
questions.correct_rationale: Legacy logging needs a bucket with ACLs enabled, and a separate log bucket leaves ACLs disabled on the asset bucket.
distractor_rationales: A bucket policy does not help, because legacy delivery depends on ACLs that bucket owner enforced disables.
Enabling ACLs on the asset bucket would restore delivery but breaks the rule that ACLs stay disabled there.
Logs would arrive, but the team must keep legacy standard logging with delivery to an S3 bucket.
questions.distractor_summary: WA leaves legacy S3 delivery; WB re-enables ACLs on the asset bucket; X adds a policy that ACL delivery ignores.

questions.subdomain: 1.3 Troubleshoot security monitoring, logging, and alerting solutions
questions.question: A company signs a Route 53 public hosted zone with DNSSEC, and a key signing problem went unnoticed until resolvers began failing validation. The on-call team must be notified when a key signing key needs action or an internal signing failure occurs. The team does not want to write or run code that polls the zone status. What should the team set up?
options: A Route 53 health check against the website endpoint, with a CloudWatch alarm that notifies on-call when the check fails.
A scheduled Lambda function that calls GetDNSSEC for the zone and notifies the on-call team when the signing status changes.
An EventBridge rule on CloudTrail events for ChangeResourceRecordSets calls in the zone, which notifies the on-call team by email.
CloudWatch alarms on the zone's DNSSECInternalFailure and DNSSECKeySigningKeysNeedingAction metrics that notify an SNS topic.
questions.correct_rationale: These alarms fire on internal signing failures and on key signing keys that need action, and they need no polling code.
distractor_rationales: A health check tests the endpoint, not whether DNSSEC signing has failed or a key needs action.
Polling GetDNSSEC detects status changes, but it is code the team does not want to write or run.
Record changes are logged, but signing failures and key actions are not record set changes.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design and test an incident response plan
questions.question: A company wants an AWS service that triages its GuardDuty and Security Hub CSPM findings on its behalf and supports the incident lifecycle through containment and recovery guidance. Which service meets this need?
options: AWS Security Hub CSPM automation rules, which update or suppress findings that match criteria the security team defines.
AWS Security Incident Response, which triages findings from existing detection sources and guides containment and recovery.
AWS Trusted Advisor, which checks accounts against best practices and reports security recommendations for the team to act on.
Amazon Detective, which builds behavior graphs from log data so that analysts can investigate the root cause of findings.
questions.correct_rationale: Security Incident Response ingests findings from existing sources, triages them, and covers containment and recovery guidance.
distractor_rationales: Automation rules update findings by criteria; they do not triage or guide incident containment.
Trusted Advisor reports best-practice checks, not triage of security findings.
Detective supports investigation by analysts but does not triage findings on the company's behalf.
questions.distractor_summary: Detective aids analyst investigation; automation rules edit findings; Trusted Advisor checks best practices.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design and test an incident response plan
questions.question: A company subscribes to AWS Shield Advanced for its CloudFront distributions and Application Load Balancers, and its account is on the Developer Support plan. During a DDoS event, Shield Response Team engineers must be able to review and update the AWS WAF rules that protect these resources. The incident response plan must make sure the company is eligible to engage the Shield Response Team at all. What should the plan include?
options: Authorize the Shield Response Team with a role that can manage the AWS WAF rules, and keep the account on the Developer Support plan.
Move the account to the Business Support plan or higher, and authorize the Shield Response Team with a role that can manage the AWS WAF rules.
Rely on Shield Standard protections for the distributions and load balancers, and have the team adjust AWS WAF rules during an event.
Move the account to the Business Support plan or higher, and open a support case for general DDoS guidance without granting any access.
questions.correct_rationale: SRT engagement requires Business or Enterprise Support, and the authorized role lets the SRT manage the WAF rules during an event.
distractor_rationales: The role gives access, but the Developer Support plan does not make the company eligible to engage the SRT.
Shield Standard does not include SRT engagement, so no SRT engineer would review the rules.
The plan upgrade makes the company eligible, but without an authorized role the SRT cannot update the WAF rules.
questions.distractor_summary: WA stays on Developer Support; WB grants the SRT no access; X has no SRT at all.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design and test an incident response plan
questions.question: A company is writing a ransomware recovery plan for workloads protected by AWS Backup in a production account. Backups must be locked in compliance mode so that no one, including a compromised administrator, can delete them early. Recovery must be possible directly from a separate recovery account without running copy jobs into that account. Which design meets these requirements?
options: Apply a long retention period in the production account's backup plan, and restrict vault deletion with an identity policy.
Store backups in a logically air-gapped vault, which is locked in compliance mode, and share it with the recovery account through AWS RAM.
Store backups in a standard vault in the production account with AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode applied to that vault.
Copy recovery points each day from the production account into an unlocked standard vault in the recovery account for restores.
questions.correct_rationale: A logically air-gapped vault carries a compliance-mode lock and can be shared through AWS RAM so the recovery account restores directly.
distractor_rationales: Retention settings and identity policies can be changed by a compromised administrator, so backups are not locked.
The compliance lock protects the backups, but restoring from the recovery account would need copies into that account.
Daily copies reach the recovery account, but the vault there is unlocked and recovery depends on copy jobs.
questions.distractor_summary: WA locks but needs copies; WB copies into an unlocked vault; X relies on changeable settings.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design and test an incident response plan
questions.question: A company's incident response plan requires investigators to prove that CloudTrail log files in Amazon S3 were not modified or deleted after delivery. The proof must rest on cryptographic evidence that the investigators can check themselves. Investigators must also be able to detect log files that are missing rather than altered. What should the company configure?
options: Turn on log file integrity validation for the trail, and validate log files against the signed digest files when needed.
Record the ETag of each log file in a DynamoDB table when it is delivered, and compare the stored ETags during an investigation.
Turn on S3 Versioning for the log bucket so that investigators can compare each log file with its earlier object versions.
Encrypt the log files with SSE-KMS using a customer managed key whose key policy limits which principals can decrypt them.
questions.correct_rationale: Integrity validation produces signed digest files that show whether each log file was modified, deleted, or unchanged.
distractor_rationales: Stored ETags are custom records without a signature, so they are weaker evidence and need code to maintain.
Versions show earlier copies, but they give no signed proof and do not reveal files deleted along with their versions.
Encryption controls who can read the logs; it does not prove whether files were changed or deleted.
questions.distractor_summary: WA keeps versions without signatures; WB stores unsigned ETags; X encrypts without proving integrity.

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Respond to security events
questions.question: During an incident, the response team must hand an EBS snapshot of a compromised instance to a forensics account, and the snapshot is encrypted with a customer managed KMS key. Analysts in the forensics account must be able to create a volume from the snapshot. No snapshot in the Region may be shared publicly, even by mistake during the response. Which actions should the team take?
options: Share the snapshot with the forensics account and turn on block public access for snapshots, leaving the key policy unchanged.
Make the snapshot public for a short time so that the forensics account can copy it, then make it private again.
Share the snapshot with the forensics account, allow that account to use the customer managed key, and turn on block public access for snapshots.
Share the snapshot with the forensics account and allow that account to use the customer managed key in the key policy.
questions.correct_rationale: The forensics account needs both the snapshot permission and use of the key, and block public access stops public sharing in the Region.
distractor_rationales: Without access to the customer managed key, the forensics account cannot create a volume from the encrypted snapshot.
Public sharing is exactly what must not happen, even for a short time.
This lets analysts create a volume, but nothing prevents a snapshot in the Region from being shared publicly.
questions.distractor_summary: WA withholds the key; WB omits block public access; X shares publicly.

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Respond to security events
questions.question: A company wants EC2 instances named in GuardDuty findings about compromised instances to be isolated by swapping their security groups. Isolation must start without a person taking action. Isolation must begin shortly after each finding is generated, not on a fixed schedule. Which design meets these requirements?
options: An AWS Config rule that evaluates the instance's security groups each day and flags instances named in GuardDuty findings.
An EventBridge rule that matches GuardDuty finding events and invokes a Lambda function to swap the instance's security groups.
An hourly scheduled Lambda function that lists new GuardDuty findings and swaps the security groups of the named instances.
An SNS topic subscribed to the GuardDuty findings that emails the on-call engineer, who then swaps the instance's security groups.
questions.correct_rationale: EventBridge receives each finding as it is generated and invokes the function, so isolation is automatic and prompt.
distractor_rationales: A daily evaluation is neither prompt nor an isolation action, and it does not read GuardDuty findings.
The function acts without a person, but an hourly schedule delays isolation instead of reacting to each finding.
The email arrives quickly, but a person must still swap the security groups.
questions.distractor_summary: WA polls on a schedule; WB needs a person; X evaluates daily and does not isolate.

docLinks.title: Processing GuardDuty findings with Amazon EventBridge

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Respond to security events
questions.question: Many engineers federate from a corporate identity provider into a shared role, and investigators cannot tell from CloudTrail which person performed each action. Investigators must be able to identify the person behind every action taken in the assumed-role sessions. The person's identity must stay attached when an engineer chains from the shared role into another role. What should the security team do?
options: Require the identity provider to set a source identity from the user's corporate name, and review the source identity in CloudTrail events.
Require the identity provider to set the role session name to the user's corporate name, and review session names in CloudTrail.
Create an IAM Access Analyzer external access analyzer that reports which principals can assume the shared role from outside.
Turn on CloudTrail data events for every S3 bucket and Lambda function so that investigators see more detail about each action.
questions.correct_rationale: A source identity is present in requests for every action in the session and persists when the engineer chains into another role.
distractor_rationales: Session names help, but each later role assumption can set a different session name, so the person is lost when chaining.
External access findings show who can assume the role from outside, not who performed each action.
More events give more detail, but they still show the shared role session rather than the person.
questions.distractor_summary: WA uses changeable session names; WB adds events without the person; X reports external access.

questions.subdomain: 3.1 Design, implement, and troubleshoot security controls for network edge services
questions.question: A company protects an Application Load Balancer with AWS WAF and must stop requests that originate from one region within a country. Requests from every other region of that country must still reach the application. The security team will not build or maintain lists of IP addresses for the rule. Which rule design meets these requirements?
options: A CloudFront geographic restriction in front of the load balancer that denies the country in which the region is located.
An IP set rule with a block action that holds the address ranges assigned to the region, updated by the team as those ranges change.
A geo match rule for the country, which labels requests by region, followed by a label match rule that blocks the region's label.
A geo match rule for the country with a block action, so that requests from the region and the rest of the country are stopped.
questions.correct_rationale: The geo match statement labels requests with their region, and a label match rule can block that one region while the rest pass.
distractor_rationales: CloudFront geographic restriction works at the country level, so it blocks the entire country.
Address ranges can target the region, but the team will not maintain IP lists.
Blocking the country as a whole stops the region but also stops the other regions that must still reach the application.
questions.distractor_summary: WA blocks the whole country; WB maintains IP lists; X restricts at the country level.

questions.subdomain: 3.1 Design, implement, and troubleshoot security controls for network edge services
questions.question: A web form posts payment card numbers through CloudFront to an origin whose application servers pass the data to a payment service. The card number must be encrypted at the edge and stay encrypted until the payment service decrypts it with its private key. Application servers must still read the other form fields, such as name and shipping address, in plaintext. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Configure CloudFront field-level encryption for the card number field with the payment service's public key, leaving other fields unchanged.
Encrypt the entire POST body at the edge with a Lambda@Edge function so that application servers forward the body to the payment service.
Add an AWS WAF rule that inspects the POST body and blocks requests in which a card number appears in plaintext.
Set the origin protocol policy to HTTPS so that the card number and every other field are encrypted between CloudFront and the origin.
questions.correct_rationale: Field-level encryption encrypts the named field at the edge with the public key, while other fields reach the servers as plaintext.
distractor_rationales: Encrypting the whole body protects the card number but hides the name and address from the servers.
Blocking requests does not encrypt the card number; it stops valid orders.
HTTPS protects the hop to the origin, but the servers then see the card number in plaintext.
questions.distractor_summary: WA encrypts transport only; WB encrypts every field; X blocks instead of encrypting.

questions.subdomain: 3.1 Design, implement, and troubleshoot security controls for network edge services
questions.question: A company distributes training videos to a partner through CloudFront from a private S3 origin. Each download link must stop working after a set expiry time. Links must work from the partner's office IP address range and fail from anywhere else. Which approach meets these requirements?
options: Issue CloudFront signed URLs with a custom policy that sets the expiry time and the partner's office IP address range.
Issue CloudFront signed URLs with a canned policy that sets an expiry time for each video file that the partner downloads.
Keep the video URLs unsigned, and attach an AWS WAF IP set rule to the distribution that allows the partner's office range.
Issue S3 presigned URLs for the video objects so that the partner downloads them directly from the bucket before they expire.
questions.correct_rationale: A custom policy can include an expiry time and the IP range of the users who may access the content.
distractor_rationales: A canned policy sets an expiry but cannot restrict the IP address range.
The IP set limits the source range, but unsigned URLs do not expire.
Presigned URLs expire, but they bypass CloudFront and do not restrict the office IP range.
questions.distractor_summary: WA lacks the IP limit; WB never expires; X bypasses CloudFront without the IP limit.

docLinks.title: Use signed URLs

questions.subdomain: 3.2 Design, implement, and troubleshoot security controls for compute workloads
questions.question: A company has 40 accounts in AWS Organizations across five Regions and wants one patching approach for every managed node. Security must define the patch baseline and schedule once, rather than in each account and Region. Accounts added to the organization later must be patched under the same configuration. Which approach meets these requirements?
options: Create a State Manager association that runs AWS-RunPatchBaseline from the management account in each Region that the company uses.
Create a Quick Setup patch policy for the organization that sets the baseline and schedule for nodes in every account and Region.
Create a maintenance window with a patching task in each account and Region, with the same baseline defined in every one of them.
Turn on Amazon Inspector for the organization so that missing patches on managed nodes are reported to the security team.
questions.correct_rationale: A patch policy for the organization defines the baseline and schedule once and applies to managed nodes across accounts and Regions.
distractor_rationales: An association targets one account and Region pair, so it does not reach member accounts or later ones.
Maintenance windows target one account and Region pair, so the configuration is repeated rather than defined once.
Inspector reports missing patches but does not install them.
questions.distractor_summary: WA repeats per account and Region; WB stays in one account; X reports without patching.

docLinks.title: Patch policy configurations in Quick Setup

questions.subdomain: 3.2 Design, implement, and troubleshoot security controls for compute workloads
questions.question: A security team wants a managed AWS service that automates building hardened, customized server images and keeping them up to date. Which service meets this need?
options: AWS Elastic Beanstalk, which deploys and scales web applications on EC2 using platform versions that AWS manages.
Amazon Inspector, which scans EC2 instances and container images for software vulnerabilities and network exposure.
EC2 Image Builder, which automates the creation, management, and deployment of customized, secure server images.
AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager, which installs operating system patches on running managed nodes in a set window.
questions.correct_rationale: Image Builder automates building, managing, and deploying customized, secure, up-to-date images.
distractor_rationales: Elastic Beanstalk deploys applications; it is not an image pipeline.
Inspector finds vulnerabilities; it does not build or update images.
Patch Manager patches running nodes; it does not build images.
questions.distractor_summary: Patch Manager patches running nodes; Inspector scans; Elastic Beanstalk deploys applications.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 Design, implement, and troubleshoot security controls for compute workloads
questions.question: A security team attached a code signing configuration that enforces signature checks to several existing Lambda functions. After the change, each function must run code signed through an approved signing profile. Some of the functions were deployed with unsigned packages before the configuration was attached. What must the team do?
options: Publish a new version of each function from its current package so that Lambda checks the signature again.
Deploy a new code package signed through an approved signing profile to each function that still runs unsigned code.
Nothing further, because attaching the configuration stops the unsigned code from running in every function at once.
Set the signature validation policy to Warn so that functions running unsigned code are flagged and then blocked.
questions.correct_rationale: Existing unsigned code keeps running until a new package is deployed, so each such function needs a signed package.
distractor_rationales: Publishing a version from the current unsigned package does not make that code signed.
Attaching the configuration checks new deployments; it does not stop unsigned code that is already running.
Warn mode logs signature problems but allows deployment, so it does not enforce signed code.
questions.distractor_summary: WA assumes running code is blocked; WB only warns; X republishes unsigned code.

docLinks.title: Using code signing to verify code integrity with Lambda

questions.subdomain: 3.3 Design and troubleshoot network security controls
questions.question: Application instances in an Auto Scaling group connect to an Amazon RDS database, and instances are replaced often with new private IP addresses. The database must accept connections from the application instances and from no other hosts in the VPC. Engineers must not update database rules when application instances are replaced. Which configuration meets these requirements?
options: Add inbound rules to the database security group for the private IP address of each running application instance.
Add an inbound rule to the database security group that references the application instances' security group.
Add a network ACL rule on the database subnets that allows the application subnets and denies all other VPC traffic.
Add an inbound rule to the database security group that allows the database port from the CIDR block of the whole VPC.
questions.correct_rationale: Referencing the application security group admits any instance that carries it, so replacements need no rule updates.
distractor_rationales: Per-address rules admit the right hosts, but they must change whenever instances are replaced.
Subnet rules admit every host in the application subnets, including ones that are not application instances.
A VPC CIDR rule needs no updates, but it admits every host in the VPC.
questions.distractor_summary: WA admits the whole VPC; WB needs updates; X admits whole subnets.

docLinks.title: Security group rules

questions.subdomain: 3.3 Design and troubleshoot network security controls
questions.question: Contractors use a client VPN today to reach several internal web applications that run behind internal load balancers. With a Deny alone, no resource has an Allow, so the Lambda updates are blocked as well.

questions.subdomain: 6.2 Implement a secure and consistent deployment strategy for cloud resources
questions.question: In AWS Service Catalog, how do administrators make approved offerings available to end users while controlling how they are provisioned?
options: They group products into portfolios, add provisioning constraints and tags, and grant IAM users and groups access to them.
They create a separate account for every product and give end users console sign-in there to deploy it by hand.
They attach a service control policy to each product so that member accounts can launch it with any parameters they choose.
They publish each product as a public template in a shared bucket and rely on bucket policies to decide who may launch it.
questions.correct_rationale: Portfolios with constraints and tags, shared to IAM principals, are how Service Catalog controls provisioning.
distractor_rationales: Separate accounts with manual deployment do not use the catalog at all.
SCPs are not attached to products, and unrestricted parameters defeat the purpose of constraints.
A public template in a bucket gives no provisioning constraints and is not how Service Catalog grants access.
questions.distractor_summary: Service Catalog = portfolios + constraints + tags + IAM access.

docLinks.title: What Is Service Catalog?

questions.subdomain: 6.2 Implement a secure and consistent deployment strategy for cloud resources
questions.question: What does AWS CloudFormation Guard let a team do with its infrastructure templates?
options: Store each template version in a managed repository and require approval before a change set is executed.
Write rules in a domain-specific policy language and validate JSON or YAML data, such as templates, against them.
Roll back a stack automatically when a deployed resource drifts from the template that created it in the account.
Convert resources that were created in the console into a template and import them into a new stack.
questions.correct_rationale: Guard is a policy-as-code tool that validates structured data against DSL rules.
distractor_rationales: Guard does not store templates or run approval workflows.
Drift detection reports drift; Guard does not roll back stacks.
Generating templates from existing resources is a different capability.
questions.distractor_summary: Guard = DSL rules validating JSON/YAML.

questions.subdomain: 6.3 Evaluate the compliance of AWS resources
questions.question: A security team wants one view of AWS Config resource and compliance data from every account in its organization, held in an audit account. New member accounts must appear in the view without each account owner approving a request. The audit account must not be able to modify configuration or rules in the source accounts. Which approach meets these needs?
options: Create an aggregator in the audit account that lists individual account IDs, then have each source account authorize it.
Have each account owner grant the audit account a role that can change AWS Config rules and settings in that account.
Deploy a role with full AWS Config permissions to each member account through service-managed StackSets and query it centrally.
Create an aggregator in the audit account that uses the organization as its source, which replicates data for viewing without per-account authorization.
questions.correct_rationale: An organization-based aggregator needs no authorization from members, picks up new accounts, and replicates data read-only.
distractor_rationales: Listing accounts requires each source account to authorize the aggregator, so new accounts need approval.
This needs per-account approval and grants the ability to change rules.
A role with full Config permissions lets the audit account modify rules in source accounts.
questions.distractor_summary: WA needs approvals; WB grants write access; X does both.
